chapters.title: How to Intrigue Everyone Without Saying a Word: You Only Have Ten Seconds to Show You're a Somebody
chapters.sourcePressure: Opening first-impression unit covering techniques 1 through 9: smile timing, sustained eye contact, visible attention, stillness, turning toward someone, greeting warmth, reduced fidgeting, situational reading, and room reading before acting.
chapters.coreMove: Set your face, body, and attention before the first sentence so the other person reads composure and welcome immediately.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating first impression as vague confidence, attractiveness, or body-language trivia.

chapters.title: How to Know What to Say After You Say "Hi"
chapters.sourcePressure: Conversation-continuation unit covering techniques 10 through 23: matching mood, giving easy hooks, using context and visible objects, richer introductions, repeated words, spotlighting, parroting, and encore prompts.
chapters.coreMove: Keep a new exchange alive by giving the other person conversational handles and returning their own words as invitations.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating conversation as clever openers or a list of canned questions.

chapters.title: How to Talk Like a VIP
chapters.sourcePressure: Verbal-status unit covering techniques 24 through 37: identity-question answers, compressed self-description, stronger words, avoiding quick imitation, cliches, teasing, overeager gratitude, and keeping attention on the receiver.
chapters.coreMove: Answer and phrase with precision and restraint so your words sound useful instead of needy.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating VIP speech as sounding expensive, dominant, or artificially polished.

chapters.title: How to Be an Insider in Any Crowd: What Are They All Talking About?
chapters.sourcePressure: Insider-entry unit covering techniques 38 through 43: learning enough vocabulary, publications, hot-button topics, customs, and bargaining language to avoid sounding lost in an unfamiliar group.
chapters.coreMove: Arrive with enough borrowed literacy to ask live questions without pretending to belong more than you do.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating insider fluency as bluffing expertise or memorizing jargon to impress people.

chapters.title: How to Sound Like You're Peas in a Pod: "Why, We're Just Alike!"
chapters.sourcePressure: Rapport-by-likeness unit covering techniques 44 through 50: mirroring, echoing, empathizing, shared imagery, and early identity language that makes people feel alike.
chapters.coreMove: Reflect the other person rhythm, words, and self-picture so likeness feels natural instead of performed.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating rapport as mimicry, fake agreement, or generic empathy.

chapters.title: How to Differentiate the Power of Praise from the Folly of Flattery
chapters.sourcePressure: Recognition unit covering techniques 51 through 59: praise, compliments, indirect recognition, repeated small affirmations, and the line between credible admiration and motive-exposing flattery.
chapters.coreMove: Make praise specific, observed, and socially believable so it strengthens identity instead of exposing your agenda.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the lesson as compliment more often or say nicer things.

chapters.title: How to Direct Dial Their Hearts
chapters.sourcePressure: Phone-presence unit covering techniques 60 through 70: vocal warmth, using the other person name, honoring interruptions and context, voicemail, openings, pacing, and replacing missing visual cues.
chapters.coreMove: Use voice, name, timing, and message shape to make a call feel like recognition instead of access.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating phone skill as polite etiquette or scripts to keep someone on the line.

chapters.title: How to Work a Party Like a Politician Works a Room: The Politician's Six-Point Party Checklist
chapters.sourcePressure: Room-working unit covering techniques 71 through 77: entering social rooms, choosing occupied or available posture, reading before moving, approaching intentionally, signaling openness, remembering, and following up.
chapters.coreMove: Move through a crowded room with deliberate attention, approach timing, openness, memory, and follow-through.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the party as transactional networking or collecting names.

chapters.title: How to Break the Most Treacherous Glass Ceiling of All: Sometimes People Are Tigers
chapters.sourcePressure: High-pressure tact unit covering techniques 78 through 92: face-saving, recovery from embarrassment, buried motives, favors and reciprocity, emotional energy, escape hatches, and status-sensitive situations.
chapters.coreMove: Give people a face-saving path when they feel exposed, cornered, indebted, emotional, or status-threatened.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating tact as generic etiquette, conflict avoidance, or strategic emotional control.
